answer: Before the British there was no modern census, only Ottoman counts of another kind. For 1914 a Turkish estimate gave about 689,000 people in all; Jews are put at 60,000 to 85,000. The British census of 1922 found 757,182 people, 83,794 of them Jews; the last census, in 1931, found about 1,035,000. By the end of 1946 the UN committee estimated the settled population at about 1,846,000: 1,203,000 Arabs and 608,000 Jews. About 376,000 Jewish immigrants were recorded from 1920 to 1946, most of the Jewish growth. The British and UN inquiries put Arab growth almost entirely down to births over deaths, but Arab immigration was not fully recorded, and a minority view says it mattered more. So the land was inhabited, mostly by Arabs: Jews were about 11 percent of the 1922 census count and a third of the 1946 settled-population estimate (not exactly the same footing).

facts.text: Before the British censuses Palestine's population is known only from Ottoman registers and outside estimates. The Mandate's Survey says no data are available on the size of the population before the British occupation; the American Jewish Year Book says Ottoman enumerations were not organised like a modern census; and a Cambridge article re-examining an actual 1849 Ottoman count of Nablus (20,000, against the 8,000-9,000 usually cited) says it raises serious doubts about commonly accepted figures. The earlier figures are therefore uncertain, and may err in either direction.

facts.text: The UN Special Committee on Palestine (UNSCOP) estimated the settled population at the end of 1946 at about 1,846,000: 1,203,000 Arabs, 608,000 Jews and 35,000 others, and warned that such estimates carry a margin of error that grows as the census year recedes. Its vital records cover the whole population except the small Bedouin group living as nomads. Its own table gives the Jewish share as 12.91 percent in 1922 and 32.96 percent in 1946, on a 1922 total of 649,048 that differs from the census count of 757,182, so the 1922 census figure and the 1946 estimate are not on exactly the same footing. The figures come from the Mandate government's statistician, so UNSCOP, the Survey and the Anglo-American Committee repeat one set of British statistics rather than confirming it independently.

facts.text: The Arab population also grew fast, and the official inquiries attributed the growth almost entirely to natural increase: the Anglo-American Committee counted only 19,000 of the Muslim population's growth of 472,000 (1922 to 1944) as immigration. facts.text: The official migration counts are incomplete: the Survey's statisticians made no allowance for illegal immigration before 1939, and name illegal immigration, mainly from neighbouring countries, as a source of error for Muslims. The demographer Roberto Bachi, quoted by the economist Fred Gottheil (Middle East Quarterly), wrote of Muslim immigration that he was unable to even guess the size of total immigration; this is second-hand. A letter by Ronald Sanders in the New York Review of Books, written in defence of Joan Peters's thesis, says the British kept thorough records of Jewish immigration but none for Arabs migrating overland.

contested.text: Joan Peters's 1984 book argued that much Arab growth was illegal immigration drawn by Zionist prosperity. Later reviewers stressed its technical, historical and literary faults; Daniel Pipes, who had praised it, does not dispute the faults but holds that neither Yehoshua Porath nor any other reviewer has refuted its central thesis. Porath, an Israeli historian (quoted here second-hand, in a letter by Ronald Sanders), held that most of the growth was natural increase, as the British and UN inquiries had found. The economist Fred Gottheil argues that unrecorded illegal immigration from 1922 to 1931 mattered. Our reading: the large majority of the growth was natural increase; some immigration and movement within the country happened but cannot be measured.

could_not_verify: Two facts have only two reliable sites: the Ottoman-era uncertainty and 1914 estimates (the American Jewish Year Book and the Survey of Palestine are both on bjpa.org, one site), and the end-of-1944 estimate. I found no third readable independent page for them.

The end-of-1946 figures: UNSCOP and the Mandate government's 1947 Supplement to the Survey (reproduced in a 1949 UN paper, whose scan is garbled) are the documents; the Supplement itself was not found online. I found no independent scholar or news page that repeats the Arab and Jewish split.

Ottoman census totals (Karpat, McCarthy) were not read; Justin McCarthy's book is under copyright and I did not cite it. The Journal of Palestine Studies demography article, UN University Press table and a mideastweb.org summary were not readable.
The 1931 census report is an unreadable scan here; its figures come from the Survey, ECF, Emory's quotation and the news item.

The Survey of Palestine and the Anglo-American report give the Jewish and Arab counts but differ in total (1,765,000 vs 1,727,786 in the American Jewish Year Book) because of how they count forces and nomads; I did not resolve it.
UNSCOP's own table of religions gives a 1922 Muslim figure (486,177) that does not match the census (590,890); I cite only its prose paragraphs.
I did not find a readable page by a demographer arguing that Arab growth from 1922 to 1946 was mostly immigration other than Gottheil on 1922-1931.

Reviewer: the best scholarly counter to Gottheil, Justin McCarthy's demographic study of Palestine's population, is only reached through Gottheil's critique of it, so it is not carried; no first-hand page for it was read.
Reviewer: nomads and the 1922 census scope: no page I could read says whether the 757,182 includes the Bedouin; UNSCOP's own table uses 649,048 for 1922.
not_claimed: This card does not say there was no Arab immigration into Palestine, only that the official inquiries put it at a small share of the growth.
It does not say the Jewish population was small in 1947; it says it was about a third.
It does not give the Arab population by origin or say how many Arab families were in their villages for generations.
It does not say the land was 'empty' or 'full': counts alone do not settle that.

skeptic.notes: Read 2+ sources for every fact (12). Checked every figure in its paragraph. Figures are accurate, but: [must-fix] Independence: from 1922 on, every count (census, Survey, Hansard, Anglo-American Committee, UNSCOP) is the Mandate government's own statistics, so the gate's three sites are one dataset. Facts 0, 1, 4, 11 have only two origins (the American Jewish Year Book and the Survey are both bjpa.org). Fact 5 has two UN pages for one UNSCOP report. Fact 6's numbers rest on one Hansard answer (government). The card cannot be called three-source on this basis. [must-fix] The old answer's last sentence mixed bases: 11 percent is of the 1922 census total, 33 percent is of the 1946 settled-population estimate; UNSCOP's own table gives 12.91 and 32.96 on a different 1922 total. Fixed in the answer and fact 5. [must-fix] Fact 0 said the Mandate statisticians called the older figures 'unreliable'; the Survey says only that no data are available. Reworded. The Cambridge article found Nablus about twice the size usually cited, so the old guesses may be too low, which matters for the Palestinian side. [must-fix] Fact 1 listed a 1900 figure under 1914 estimates and the answer called the 60,000-85,000 'Ottoman figures'; the 60,000 is an IWM video narration and 84,660 is the Survey's estimate. Reworded; the year-book quote now reads about 85,000 for 1914. [should-fix] Second-hand: Porath is quoted inside Ronald Sanders's letter, and Bachi inside Gottheil's article (about Muslim immigration, not total); both now said so in the facts and contested. Gottheil's host is the Middle East Forum (relabelled advocacy); Pipes's letter is hosted on his own site (other). 'Most reviewers rejected it' had no source; replaced. [should-fix] The 1931 total is 1,035,821 in the census report and 1,035,154 in the Survey; now shown. Fact 8's My Jewish Learning quote does not carry the numbers (only bpb and the Survey do). 'heard' (Khalidi on 1948) is not about population. Strongest objections: Palestinian side, no first-hand scholar (e.g. McCarthy) on Arab population and the Ottoman undercount; Israeli side, the Jewish share is given as 11 percent without the 1922 base problem being visible until fixed.

citer.notes: 7 answer sentences, each tied to facts. Removed: 'the best-known book making that case was heavily criticised' (only the contested field carries it, not a fact). Reworded: 'Nobody counted carefully' (Ottoman counts exist); 'Ottoman figures ... run from about 690,000' (one Turkish estimate, not a range, and the Jewish figures are not Ottoman); '1,846,000' now 'settled population'; the 11-to-33-percent sentence now names both bases; the minority-view sentence now rests on fact 11 (incomplete records) and says 'a minority view'.
